study.title: Revelation 15 - Preparation for the seven bowls of God's wrath
study.overview: This chapter shows the preparation phase for the spilling of the last pests. John sees the winners of the beast in worship, contemplates the open heavenly temple and observes the angels who receive the cups of divine wrath. The tone is solemn: judgment is not impulsive, but it comes from holiness, glory, and righteousness of God. At the same time, the saints already appear as triumphers, singing that God is true in his ways and worthy of fear and worship.

outline.title: The latest pests and winners by the glass sea
outline.explanation: The seven angels receive the seven last plagues, which complete the wrath of God. In contrast to the judgment that comes upon the earth, John sees those who have overcome the beast, his image and his mark in a position of victory and peace, represented by the sea of glass mixed with fire and the harps of God.

outline.title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
outline.explanation: The victors sing a praise that unites the history of liberation of Israel and redemption in Christ. They exalt the grandiose works of God, his righteousness, his truth, and his holiness, acknowledging that the nations will worship him when their judgments are manifest.

outline.title: The Open Temple and the Smoke of Glory
outline.explanation: The temple of the tabernacle of the testimony is opened in heaven, and the angels come out of purity to receive the bowls of wrath. The temple is filled with the smoke of the glory and power of God, indicating majesty, holy presence and the impossibility of interrupting the course of judgments until its conclusion.

study.context: The chapter belongs to the sequence of visions of the final judgments. The notes indicate that he introduces the third and last cycle of seven judgments, linked to the last seven plagues. The image of the heavenly temple resumes the language of the tabernacle and the sanctuary, where God reveals himself and governs himself. There is also an echo of God's victory by freeing his people in the midst of suffering, especially in reference to the song of Moses.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes that the judgment of God is holy, just, and complete. Divine wrath is not whim, but a final response to evil and system represented by the beast. At the same time, the redeemed are not defined by fear, but by fidelity: they remain standing, celebrating the victory of the Lamb. The song shows unity between the work of God in the old covenant and its realization in Christ. The smoke that fills the temple communicates that divine glory is holy and irresistible; no one enters to interrupt the act of judgment. Thus, the text unites comfort for the persecuted and warning to the rebels.

scholarViews.insight: The last seven plagues lead God's wrath to its final fulfillment; the chapter introduces the third and final cycle of judgments.
Those who have overcome the beast appear as witnesses to the defeat of their enemies and the full victory of God, in contrast to the destruction that will come over the anti-Christian system.
The smoke that fills the temple is a sign of the glory and power of God, remembering the consecrations of the tabernacle and the temple in the past.

questions: What changes in my posture when I remember that God's judgments are righteous and true, and not arbitrary?
In which situations am I tempted to negotiate my fidelity to the Lamb to avoid pressure or opposition?
My praise highlights the deliverances of God or his holiness, righteousness, and truth?
study.practice: This week, take time to worship God on the basis of who he is, not just what he does. When facing pressure, you consciously decide not to give in to the visible marks of a system contrary to Christ, whether for fear, advantage or approval. Reread the chapter as prayer: recognize the holiness of God, confess your righteousness and ask for perseverance to stand with the victors.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text and the notes provided do not explain in detail who exactly the winners are, nor do they develop the symbolic nature of the glass sea beyond what the notes say. It is also not possible to affirm with certainty, only with this material, the specific historical identity of the beast or the antichrist, since the commentators speak in interpretive and non-unanimous terms.
